items.prompt: Explain why an income average and a sanitation-access measure answer different questions.
items.canonical_answer: Income describes a resource average (1), whereas sanitation access describes a particular service condition, so one does not fully replace the other (1).
marking_guidance: Difference/distinguishing test: resource versus service dimension,1 each.

items.prompt: Explain why an invented region with higher income per head can still have poor service access for some residents.
items.canonical_answer: The income average can conceal unequal distribution or local barriers (1), so it does not show each household’s meaningful access to the service (1).
marking_guidance: Context: region; reasoning: average/access difference 1; result: group outcome limited 1.

items.prompt: Explain why real total income rising 5 percent does not prove higher real income per head if population also rises 5 percent.
items.canonical_answer: The denominator rises in the same proportion (1), so the average is unchanged even though the real total is larger (1).
marking_guidance: Confusion: total versus per head; boundary/test: divide by population,1 each.

items.prompt: An invented economy has real income N$120 million and 20,000 people, later N$126 million and 21,000. A service-access average improves, but a remote group remains poorly served. No distribution or quality details are supplied. (a) Describe three relevant features (6). (b) Examine what the measures show about living standards (7). (c) Suggest a better evidence-based comparison (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Real total rises 5 percent. Population also rises 5 percent. Income per head stays N$6,000 while the aggregate access measure and local experience differ. (b) More total resources do not show a higher average per person. The service average can improve without equivalent gains for the remote group. Distribution, quality and reliability are missing, so individual welfare improvements cannot be inferred. (c) Compare consistent per-person measures and group access, then examine reliability, quality and relevant education/health conditions. The judgement recognises the recorded aggregate changes while asking whether gains reach people meaningfully, rather than dismissing or overstating the indicators.
marking_guidance: Context: economy. Parts/allocation: (a) total, population, average/access 2 each=6. (b) ratio mechanism 3, distribution/service limits 4=7. (c) comparable data 3, wider outcomes 2, conditional judgement 2=7. Mechanism: access and distribution determine usable benefits; judgement requires actual group outcomes.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: (a) Define real income per head (2). (b) Define life expectancy at birth (2). (c) Explain why an average does not describe each person (2). (d) Explain enrolment versus learning attainment (2). (e) Explain service coverage versus reliability (2). (f) Define the digital divide (2). (g) Explain one reason for disparities within an economy (2). (h) Explain why multiple indicators help (2).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Price-adjusted income/population. (b) Average survival years for a newborn under prevailing age-specific mortality conditions. (c) Different distributions can share a mean. (d) Participation does not establish what is learned. (e) A connection or coverage criterion does not show continuous useful service. (f) Unequal technology access/use. (g) Access, skills or employment can differ between regions/groups. (h) Different dimensions and limits are revealed rather than hidden by one total.
marking_guidance: Parts/allocation and precision: eight at 2. (a) real aggregate + denominator; (b) average + conditional mortality basis; (c) mean + distribution; (d) stages contrasted; (e) scope/reliability; (f) inequality + access/use; (g) mechanism + condition difference; (h) dimensions + complementary evidence.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: An invented region provides digital public information. Connected residents save journeys, but some households cannot afford access and training support is limited. The authority proposes declaring improved living standards solely from device numbers. (a) Define the digital divide (2). (b) Explain two possible benefits of usable technology (4). (c) Explain why effects differ between households (7). (d) Discuss the proposed success measure (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Unequal access to or ability to use information technology/services. (b) Useful remote information can save travel and make assistance easier to reach. Communication can support learning or productive opportunities when relevant and usable. (c) Affordability, reliability and skills constrain use, so a device count can coexist with exclusion. The connected group gains convenience while others may lose a practical route if alternatives disappear. Real outcomes also depend on the information’s usefulness and ability to act. (d) Device numbers describe an input, not full meaningful access or welfare. Measure use, service reliability, costs and outcomes across groups. Declare a supported improvement where actual benefits reach intended residents at an acceptable resource cost, retaining alternatives for those excluded; the count alone is insufficient.
marking_guidance: Context: digital service. Parts/allocation: (a) unequal access 1, use capability 1. (b) two opportunity mechanisms 2 each=4. (c) cost/skills 3, distribution 2, usefulness 2=7. (d) count usefulness 2, missing outcome dimensions 2, conditional judgement 3=7. Mechanism: access and distribution determine usable benefits; judgement requires actual group outcomes.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Evaluate whether an invented analyst should describe living standards as uniformly high solely from a high national real-income-per-head figure (9).
items.canonical_answer: For: a high real average indicates substantial measured resources per person on the stated basis and can support useful consumption and services. Against: distribution, population groups, public access, education, survival and environmental conditions may differ. A mean is not each person’s income and a single dimension is incomplete. Judgement: use the real average as one relevant indicator alongside group distribution and non-income outcomes. The condition for a uniform claim is evidence about residents’ actual conditions across the relevant dimensions, which the average alone does not provide.
marking_guidance: Argument for: resource information up to 4. Argument against: distribution/non-income limits up to 4. Judgement: distinct group-and-dimension evidence condition 1. Total 9. Condition: comparable evidence across people and dimensions must support the wider claim.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum
